Trump’s ICE Assault Cases: Built for Intimidation, Not Convictions

Trump’s immigration war runs on a simple move: agents yell “18 U.S.C. 111!” while smashing windows, tackling protesters and dragging immigrants out of cars — then call it “assault on a federal officer.” The data now shows how thin that is.

More than 550 people have been charged under that statute in ICE and Border Patrol operations. Of over 400 resolved cases, nearly half collapsed: juries acquitted, judges tossed charges, or prosecutors backed off. In normal federal criminal practice, the government wins more than 90 percent of the time; here, it’s closer to a coin flip.

What kills these cases isn’t clever lawyering, it’s video. Again and again, clips show agents as the first to use force — shoving, tackling, pepper‑spraying, smashing car windows — then charging whoever screamed or resisted. 

Judges have caught agents destroying or hiding evidence, from repairing damaged government cars before defense experts could inspect them to making a young woman delete photos from her phone, including the “Recently Deleted” folder. 

At least two judges ruled evidence was deliberately destroyed, violating defendants’ rights.

The statute itself requires forcible assault or interference. Biden’s DOJ used it against Jan. 6 rioters and didn’t lose a case until Trump returned and pardoned them. 

Under Trump, ICE and Border Patrol turned it into a general‑purpose weapon against protest and observation: people were charged for filming, following, honking, blowing whistles, or yelling “La migra is coming,” with no physical contact alleged. 

In more than 100 cases, prosecutors never claimed any agent was hurt; in others, injuries came from officers’ own actions, like glass from windows they broke themselves.

The stories are variations on one theme. Two mothers in Charlotte try to warn neighbors about an ICE sweep, end up trapped on a dead‑end street, screaming into a 911 call as a rifle barrel smashes their SUV window. 

They’re charged with “impeding,” celebrated online as “excellent arrests,” then quietly cleared when the U.S. attorney drops the case. A school staffer in Minneapolis is shoved, tackled and choked for moving toward a crowd watching an arrest; his “assault” charge is first reduced, then abandoned when video doesn’t match the official story. An undocumented Honduran in Laredo, barely five feet tall, is prosecuted for punching a much larger officer; body‑cam shows the officer grabbing him by the neck, forcing him down and punching him. The jury acquits; he’s slated for deportation anyway.

Officials claim they’re facing a “massive increase” in threats and are right to “prioritize” these prosecutions. The record suggests something else: a law repurposed as a fear lever, a dragnet for anyone who gets near immigration raids, and a trail of discarded cases and judicial opinions describing ICE and DOJ behavior as “flagrant,” “in bad faith,” and “shocking to the universal sense of justice.”

Yes, some people really assaulted agents, and many others took plea deals. But when almost every contested case breaks under basic scrutiny, you’re not seeing law and order. You’re seeing a government trying to criminalize resistance and calling it protection for federal officers.

🔔 Bitcoin price nears Fidelity’s power law support: Accumulation zone or missing catalyst? 

📌 On his power law model, a logarithmic chart that bounds Bitcoin’s entire price history between an upper resistance curve, a middle trendline, and a lower support curve, the floor currently sits near 58,000 dollars. That lower line has caught every major Bitcoin bottom since 2015. Timmer’s label for the zone the market has now entered is unambiguous: accumulation. His caveat is just as unambiguous: he sees no catalyst for a reversal, and he is not calling a bottom.

⚠️ That combination, a historically reliable floor approaching and a strategist refusing to ring the bell, is the most honest summary of the Bitcoin market in July 2026. The asset is coming off its worst quarter since the 2022 bear market, spot ETFs just recorded their largest quarterly outflow since launch, the speculative premium that carried the price past 120,000 dollars last year has evaporated, and the fast money has visibly rotated elsewhere, first into gold, then into semiconductor stocks. And yet the two quantitative measures Timmer trusts most, the deviation from the power law trendline and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio, have both sunk to depths recorded at exactly two prior moments: the 2018 low and the 2022 low. Both of those moments were generational buying opportunities. Both also felt like the end of the world at the time.

🔖 This feature takes the model seriously in both directions: what the power law actually says, why its track record earns attention, and why the missing-catalyst objection is not a hedge but the core of the analysis.
